meta.title: Why pressing the lift button five times still brings **one lift**
meta.subject: Making payment webhooks safe to retry
meta.one_liner: Retrying is easy. Retrying without doing things twice is the real trick.

goal: By the end you can explain why trying again can charge a customer twice, and the two ideas that stop it.
hook: Apps resend messages all the time when the internet hiccups. So why don't you get charged twice every time it happens?

concepts.name: Retries with backoff
concepts.explain: Think about calling a friend who doesn't pick up. You don't redial every second. You wait a minute, then five, then ten. Software does the same. **Retries with backoff** means trying a failed request again, and waiting a little longer before each new try, so a busy server gets room to recover instead of being buried under repeats.

in_your_work.text: Your shop's payment provider sent the same "payment received" message twice. The first time, your app was slow to reply, so the provider assumed the message was lost and tried again. That second message wasn't a bug in the provider. It was a retry doing exactly its job, and it's the reason your app now has to be ready for the same message arriving more than once.

concepts.story: You tap Pay on a shopping app just as the lift doors close and your signal drops. The app waits, hears nothing back, and has a choice to make: give up and tell you it failed, or quietly try again?

visual.title: What the app does when nothing comes back
visual.caption: Each wait is longer than the last, and the repeat carries the same ID.

concepts.real_world: Payment companies such as Razorpay and Stripe tell a shop about every payment by sending it a message. If the shop's app doesn't answer, they don't give up after one try. They send the same message again a few seconds later, then a minute later, then an hour later, and keep going for up to a few days. Because the gaps keep growing, a shop that was down for a while gets back on its feet before the messages pile up.
pitfalls: Assuming each message arrives exactly once. With retries, the honest promise is "at least once", so plan for repeats.
Retrying instantly in a tight loop. A struggling server then gets hammered harder, so always wait longer between tries.
concepts.fun_fact: The idea of waiting longer after each failure was popularised by Ethernet in the 1970s. When two computers talked over the same cable at once, each waited a random, growing amount of time before trying again.

concepts.name: Idempotency
concepts.explain: Think of a lift button. Press it once, or five times because you're late, and one lift comes. Extra presses change nothing. **Idempotency** is that property for software: doing an action twice has the same effect as doing it once. The usual trick is a unique ID on every request, so a repeat can be spotted and skipped.

visual.title: Same payment arrives twice
visual.caption: The second copy is the same message. Only one side notices.

in_your_work.text: Your payment handler now keeps a list of every payment message it has already handled, using the ID that comes with each one. When a message shows up again, the handler checks the list, sees the ID, and simply skips it. So even if the payment provider resends a message five times, the customer's order is marked as paid once and nobody is charged twice.

concepts.story: The retry worked, but there's a catch. The first payment had actually gone through; only the reply got lost. Now the same payment has arrived twice. Should you be charged ₹500 or ₹1,000?
concepts.real_world: When a shop asks Stripe to charge a card, it can attach a unique key to that request, a bit like a token number. If the network hiccups and the shop sends the same charge again, Stripe sees the same key, recognises the repeat, and returns the result of the first charge instead of taking the money twice. Banks and UPI apps use the same trick, which is why a resent payment request doesn't empty your account.
pitfalls: Giving every retry a brand new ID. The receiver then can't tell it's a repeat, so the protection does nothing.
Forgetting the IDs too soon. If the record is cleared before the sender stops retrying, a late repeat slips through.

concepts.name: Transactions
concepts.explain: Picture the last ticket for a concert. Two fans click Buy at the same instant. The box office has to check the seat and hand it over in one move, or both fans walk away with the same seat. A **transaction** works like that box office: a group of changes that all happen together or not at all.

steps.label: Both try to save the ID

in_your_work.text: In your app, saving a payment message's ID and updating the order now happen together in one database step. If two copies of the same message arrive at the very same moment, only one of them can save the ID. That one updates the order; the other is turned away. So the order can never be marked as paid twice, even when the copies race each other.

concepts.story: One more twist. What if both copies of the payment arrive at the very same moment? Each one checks "have I seen this before?", each one hears "no", and both go ahead.
concepts.real_world: When you book a seat on an airline or cinema app, the seat is locked and sold in a single step inside the company's database. If two people tap the same seat at the same moment, the database lets exactly one of those bookings finish and turns the other away with a "seat no longer available" message. Without that single step, both people would get a confirmation and one of them would find someone in their seat.
pitfalls: Checking "have I seen this?" first and doing the work in a separate step. The tiny gap between them is exactly where duplicates sneak in.
Treating a rare race as impossible. With enough traffic, two copies landing at the same moment will happen.
concepts.fun_fact: Banks have used the "all or nothing" rule for decades. A transfer either takes money out of one account and puts it into the other, or does neither, so money is never lost halfway.

quiz.question: A server did the work but crashed before replying. What will a well-behaved sender do?

options.why: The sender never got a reply, so it can't know that.

options.text: Send the same message again after a pause
options.why: No reply looks like failure, so it retries with backoff.

options.text: Send a brand-new message with a new ID
options.why: Retries resend the same message. A new ID would hide that it's a repeat.

quiz.question: Which of these actions is idempotent?

options.text: Add one item to the cart
options.why: Doing it twice leaves two items.

options.text: Set the user's plan to Pro
options.why: After the first time, repeating it changes nothing.

quiz.question: Two copies of one payment arrive at the same millisecond. What stops a double charge?

options.why: Timing tricks shrink the gap; they don't close it.

options.text: Saving the ID and charging in one indivisible step
options.why: Only one save can succeed, so only one charge happens.
Logs record the duplicate after it happens.

share.linkedin:
Learned something today that explains a lot of "charged twice" bugs.

Apps resend messages whenever the internet hiccups, so the same message can arrive more than once. The fix is idempotency: design actions so doing them twice has the same effect as once.

And the check has to happen in the same step as the work, or two simultaneous repeats can still slip through.

share.x: Retries make apps reliable. Idempotency makes retries safe. Doing the check and the work in one step makes it bulletproof. Learned this today with GrowthX teach.
